spec.description: Bathroom-scale arced dial with labels 60, 70 and 80 kg, one-kilogram ticks, and pointer two ticks after 70. Decorative body colours omitted.
spec.mathematics: Ten equal intervals between 70 and 80; indicated reading 72 kg.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied pointer and identifying arrow retained; no answer annotation.

answer.worked: The ten intervals between 70 and 80 each represent $1\text{ kg}$. The pointer is two intervals after 70: $70+2=72\text{ kg}$.

spec.description: Offset ruler segment labelled 11–15 cm with millimetre ticks; arrow at third subdivision after 13. Decorative fill omitted.
spec.answerVisibility: Scale and supplied identifying arrow only.

answer.worked: Each small interval is $0.1\text{ cm}$. The arrow points three intervals after 13, giving $13+0.3=13.3\text{ cm}$.

spec.description: Kitchen scale with labelled 100, 200 and 300 gram marks, ten-gram minor divisions and pointer two divisions after 200. Pan and contents retained as outline; decorative body fill omitted.
spec.answerVisibility: Original pointer, arrow and graduations only.

answer.worked: The ten intervals from 200 to 300 each represent $10\text{ g}$. The pointer is two intervals after 200: $200+2\times10=220\text{ g}$.

spec.description: Jug with horizontal liquid surface, 200–1000 mL labels and four subdivisions per 200 mL; surface at first tick above 600. Light blue fill represents liquid.
spec.mathematics: Each subdivision is 50 mL; surface 650 mL.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied liquid surface and identifying arrow visible; no added answer label.

answer.worked: Four equal intervals represent $200\text{ mL}$, so each interval is $200\div4=50\text{ mL}$. The liquid is one interval above 600: $600+50=650\text{ mL}$.

content.prompt: Calculate:

children.label: a
children.prompt: the number of square centimetres in a square metre

answer.worked:
A square metre is a square with side length $100\text{ cm}$.

$$\begin{align*}A&=100\times100\text{ cm}^2\\A&=10\,000\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: the number of hectares in a square kilometre

answer.worked:
A square kilometre is a square with side length $1000\text{ m}$, and $1\text{ ha}=10\,000\text{ m}^2$.

$$\begin{align*}A&=1000\times1000\text{ m}^2\\A&=1\,000\,000\text{ m}^2\\A&=\frac{1\,000\,000}{10\,000}\text{ ha}\\A&=100\text{ ha}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: the number of square metres in a square kilometre

answer.worked:
A square kilometre is a square with side length $1000\text{ m}$.

$$\begin{align*}A&=1000\times1000\text{ m}^2\\A&=1\,000\,000\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.methodNote: Interpret square units as squares of the corresponding side length, calculate area using length times width, and divide square metres by 10,000 to obtain hectares.

spec.answerVisibility: All figures and labels are permanent question givens; no proof or answer is shown.

answer.short: Triangles $FBA$ and $ECD$ have equal areas. Replacing $ECD$ with $FBA$ gives rectangle $AFED$, so the parallelogram has area $bh$.
answer.worked:
Since $BC=AD=FE$ and $BE$ is common, $FB=EC$. Also, $AF=ED=h$, so triangles $FBA$ and $ECD$ have equal bases and perpendicular heights, and therefore equal areas.

Move triangle $ECD$ to fill triangle $FBA$. This forms rectangle $AFED$ without changing the area.

$$\begin{align*}\operatorname{Area}(ABCD)&=\operatorname{Area}(AFED)\\\operatorname{Area}(ABCD)&=AD\times AF\\\operatorname{Area}(ABCD)&=bh.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Sarah takes 4 hours and 45 minutes to read a 200-page novel, while Derek takes 5 hours and 2 minutes. Now they both read a 300-page novel. If they read at the same speeds as for the previous novel, how much faster than Derek will Sarah finish the 300-page novel?

answer.short:
25 minutes 30 seconds earlier (1530 seconds).

Use each reader’s time per page to find their time for 300 pages, then compare.
answer.worked:
Convert the original reading times to minutes:

$$\begin{align*}\text{Sarah's time for 200 pages}&=4\times60+45=285\text{ min}\\\text{Derek's time for 200 pages}&=5\times60+2=302\text{ min}\end{align*}$$

Find the time for one page, then multiply by 300:

$$\begin{align*}\text{Sarah's time for 1 page}&=\frac{285}{200}\text{ min}\\\text{Sarah's time for 300 pages}&=\frac{285}{200}\times300=427.5\text{ min}\\\text{Derek's time for 1 page}&=\frac{302}{200}\text{ min}\\\text{Derek's time for 300 pages}&=\frac{302}{200}\times300=453\text{ min}\\\text{Time difference}&=453-427.5=25.5\text{ min}\\\text{Time difference}&=25\text{ min }30\text{ s}=1530\text{ s}\end{align*}$$

Sarah finishes 25 minutes 30 seconds earlier.

content.prompt: Calculate the perimeter and area of each of these figures, assuming that the non-slanting lines are either horizontal or vertical.

spec.description: Unshaded orthogonal polygon with a downward rectangular projection. All eleven printed dimensions are retained; the right side of the downward projection remains unlabelled. Ordinary source-blue outlines are rendered black under house style.
spec.answerVisibility: Question shows only the source givens; the missing length and calculated results appear only in answers.

answer.short:
$P=42\text{ m}$; $A=68\text{ m}^2$.

Find the missing vertical side, then add the boundary lengths and split the area into rectangles.
answer.worked:
The unlabelled vertical side is $5\text{ m}$ because its endpoints are level with those of the labelled $5\text{ m}$ side.
$$\begin{align*}P&=6+1+3+3+1+4+2+5+3+5+3+6\\P&=42\text{ m}.\end{align*}$$
For the area, take the upper enclosing $9\text{ m}\times7\text{ m}$ rectangle, subtract the upper-left $6\text{ m}\times1\text{ m}$ gap and lower-right $1\text{ m}\times4\text{ m}$ gap, then add the downward $3\text{ m}\times5\text{ m}$ rectangle.
$$\begin{align*}A&=9\times7-6\times1-1\times4+3\times5\\A&=63-6-4+15\\A&=68\text{ m}^2.\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Three adjoining right triangles retain the stepped outer boundary, three 10 km sloping sides, all printed dimensions and two internal red dashed 2 km segments. Ordinary source-blue edges are rendered black; construction red uses the standard palette. No shading.
spec.mathematics: Top triangle has perpendicular sides 6 and 8 km; left triangle has perpendicular sides 8 and 6 km; bottom triangle has perpendicular sides 8 and 6 km. The shared internal segments are each 2 km and are excluded from perimeter.
spec.answerVisibility: All source dimensions and construction segments are permanent givens. No calculated answers appear in the question figure.

answer.short:
$P=64\text{ km}$; $A=72\text{ km}^2$.

Exclude the dashed internal segments from the perimeter and add the areas of the three right triangles.
answer.worked:
Only the solid outer boundary contributes to the perimeter; the two dashed $2\text{ km}$ segments are internal.
$$\begin{align*}P&=6+10+6+4+6+10+6+6+10\\P&=64\text{ km}.\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Combines direct volume calculation, inverse use of the volume formula with mixed units, and recovery of dimensions from three face areas.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with dimensions $5.2\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}\times10\text{ cm}$.

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}V&=lwh\\V&=5.2\times6\times10\\V&=312\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A right rectangular prism has volume $625\text{ mm}^3$. The height of the prism is $12.5\text{ cm}$. Find the area of the base.

answer.worked:
Use consistent units: $12.5\text{ cm}=125\text{ mm}$. Since $V=Ah$,
$$\begin{align*}A&=\frac{V}{h}\\A&=\frac{625}{125}\\A&=5\text{ mm}^2\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: The three distinct face areas of a right rectangular prism are $35\text{ cm}^2$, $50\text{ cm}^2$ and $70\text{ cm}^2$. Find the volume of the prism.

answer.short:
$350\text{ cm}^3$.

The dimensions are $5\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$.
answer.worked:
The dimensions must give the three face areas as pairwise products. Factor pairs give
$$\begin{align*}35&=5\times7\\50&=5\times10\\70&=7\times10\end{align*}$$
Thus the dimensions are $5\text{ cm}$, $7\text{ cm}$ and $10\text{ cm}$.
$$\begin{align*}V&=lwh\\V&=5\times7\times10\\V&=350\text{ cm}^3\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Combines microsecond and century conversions to compare two large counts.

content.prompt: My dad told me that there are more microseconds in a minute than minutes in a century. Was he telling the truth?

answer.short:
Yes: there are $60\,000\,000$ microseconds in a minute and approximately $52\,560\,000$ minutes in a century.

Convert each interval to the requested unit, then compare the counts.
answer.worked:
A microsecond is $\frac{1}{1\,000\,000}$ of a second.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Microseconds in a minute}&=60\times1\,000\,000\\\text{Microseconds in a minute}&=60\,000\,000\end{align*}$$
Using $365$ days per year:

$$\begin{align*}\text{Minutes in a century}&=100\times365\times24\times60\\\text{Minutes in a century}&=52\,560\,000\end{align*}$$
Since $60\,000\,000>52\,560\,000$, he was telling the truth. Including leap days does not change this comparison.

teachingContext.methodNote: Pages 2–3 explain metric prefixes and multiplication or division by conversion factors. Page 32 gives 60 seconds per minute, 60 minutes per hour and 24 hours per day; Example 21 converts time by multiplying the relevant factors.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The question principally assesses chained time-unit conversions and comparison; identifying micro as one millionth supports the first conversion. The supplied teaching pages do not explicitly define the micro prefix, so the worked answer supplies that definition.

answerEvidence.matchEvidence: The teacher image lists Challenge exercise 1 as yes, since 6 × 10^7 > 5.256 × 10^7. These match the independently calculated 60,000,000 microseconds per minute and 52,560,000 minutes per 100 years using 365 days per year.

content.prompt: Draw three figures, based on rectangles and triangles, that have the same area but different perimeters.

answer.short:
Sample answers: a $3\text{ cm}\times2\text{ cm}$ rectangle, a $6\text{ cm}\times1\text{ cm}$ rectangle and a right triangle with perpendicular sides $3\text{ cm}$ and $4\text{ cm}$ and hypotenuse $5\text{ cm}$.

Each has area $6\text{ cm}^2$; their perimeters are $10\text{ cm}$, $14\text{ cm}$ and $12\text{ cm}$, respectively.
answer.worked:
Sample answers are shown in the figures.

For the $3\text{ cm}\times2\text{ cm}$ rectangle:
$$\begin{align*}A_1&=3\times2\\A_1&=6\text{ cm}^2\\P_1&=3+2+3+2\\P_1&=10\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
For the $6\text{ cm}\times1\text{ cm}$ rectangle:
$$\begin{align*}A_2&=6\times1\\A_2&=6\text{ cm}^2\\P_2&=6+1+6+1\\P_2&=14\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
For the right triangle:
$$\begin{align*}A_3&=\frac12\times3\times4\\A_3&=6\text{ cm}^2\\P_3&=3+4+5\\P_3&=12\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
All three areas are equal, while the three perimeters are different.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer the dimensions of a square-cornered offset boundary and combine composite areas with perimeter.

content.prompt: A path 1 metre wide is being placed around the grassed area of a garden, as shown below. What is the area of the grassed part of the garden? What is its perimeter? What will the area of the path be?

spec.description: H-shaped grass region with two 4 m wide, 3 m deep recesses; square-cornered path boundary offset by 1 m. Labels retain their source segment associations. Light blue identifies grass; dashed red distinguishes the outer path boundary.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated dimensions or answers are printed.

answer.short:
Grassed area: $120\text{ m}^2$; perimeter: $62\text{ m}$; path area: $66\text{ m}^2$.

Subtract the recesses from the enclosing rectangle, then subtract the grassed area from the area inside the outer path boundary.
answer.worked:
The enclosing grass rectangle has width $8+4+4=16\text{ m}$ and height $9\text{ m}$. Each recess measures $4\text{ m}\times3\text{ m}$.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{grass}}&=16\times9-2\times4\times3\\A_{\text{grass}}&=120\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

Each recess adds two vertical sides of $3\text{ m}$ to the enclosing rectangle's perimeter.

$$\begin{align*}P_{\text{grass}}&=2(16+9)+4\times3\\P_{\text{grass}}&=62\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

The outer boundary fits an $18\text{ m}\times11\text{ m}$ rectangle. Its two recesses are each $4-2\times1=2\text{ m}$ wide and $3\text{ m}$ deep.

$$\begin{align*}A_{\text{outer}}&=18\times11-2\times2\times3\\A_{\text{outer}}&=186\text{ m}^2\\A_{\text{path}}&=186-120\\A_{\text{path}}&=66\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$

classification.difficultyReason: Compare package prices and combine whole packages and individual cards to maximise the number within a fixed budget.

content.prompt: If birthday cards cost $\$2.50$ for a box of 12, $\$1.25$ for a packet of 3, or 50c each, what is the greatest number of cards that you can buy if you have $\$14.90$?

answer.short: 65 cards: 5 boxes, 1 packet and 2 individual cards.
answer.worked:
A box gives 12 cards for $\$2.50$. Four packets give 12 cards for $\$5.00$, while 12 individual cards cost $\$6.00$. Boxes give the lowest cost per card.

Any purchase containing at least 12 cards outside boxes can be replaced by a purchase with another box, at no greater cost and with at least as many cards. Therefore, consider purchases with fewer than 12 cards outside boxes. With four or fewer boxes, there can then be at most $4\times12+11=59$ cards.

Six boxes cost $\$15.00$, exceeding the budget. For five boxes:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Cost of five boxes}&=5\times\$2.50=\$12.50\\\text{Money remaining}&=\$14.90-\$12.50=\$2.40\end{align*}$$
Two packets cost $\$2.50$, so buy one packet and two individual cards for $\$2.25$. Without a packet, the remaining money buys only four individual cards.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Total cards}&=5\times12+3+2=65\\\text{Total cost}&=\$12.50+\$1.25+\$1.00=\$14.75\end{align*}$$
The greatest number is 65 cards.

teachingContext.methodNote: Find the cost of one item by dividing the total cost by the number of items; compare prices and use multiplication to calculate purchase costs.
teachingContext.mappingNote: The unitary-method introduction on page 8 and Example 6 on page 9 support comparing card prices. Whole-package combinations extend that method to the fixed-budget challenge.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine workforce, duration and distance at a constant working rate, then round the required workforce up to a whole person.

content.prompt: If it takes 4 people 5 days to clean up the rubbish alongside a 180 km stretch of freeway, how many people will be needed to clean 250 km of freeway in 6 days? (Assume they all work at the same pace.)

answer.short:
5 people.

Find the distance one person cleans in 6 days, then divide 250 km by that distance and round up.
answer.worked:
One person cleans the following distance in one day:
$$\begin{align*}\text{Distance per person per day}&=\frac{180}{4\times5}\\\text{Distance per person per day}&=9\text{ km}.\end{align*}$$
In 6 days, one person cleans $9\times6=54\text{ km}$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Number of people required}&=\frac{250}{54}\\\text{Number of people required}&=\frac{125}{27}=4\frac{17}{27}.\end{align*}$$
A whole number of people is needed. Round up: **5 people**.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine overlapping pair measurements, recognise that the baby is counted twice, and halve the remaining mass.

content.prompt: I took my baby to the clinic to be weighed, but he would not keep still, so I held him and stood on the scales and the weight recorded was 75 kg. Then the nurse held the baby and stood on the scales, and the weight recorded was 69 kg. Finally, the nurse and I both stood on the scales, and the weight recorded was 137 kg. What did the baby weigh?

inlines.text: Add the first two readings, subtract the adults’ combined mass, then halve.

answer.worked:
Adding the first two readings counts each adult once and the baby twice. Subtracting the adults’ combined mass leaves twice the baby’s mass.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Twice the baby's mass}&=(75+69-137)\text{ kg}\\\text{Twice the baby's mass}&=7\text{ kg}\\\text{Baby's mass}&=(7\div2)\text{ kg}\\\text{Baby's mass}&=3.5\text{ kg}\end{align*}$$

teachingContext.mappingNote: The assessed reasoning combines addition, subtraction and halving with all measurements already in kilograms; multistep arithmetic is the closest supplied skill. The authored solution explains the double counting directly rather than introducing simultaneous equations.

content.prompt: A man plants 12 rows of beans in rows that are 10 m long. The plants in each row are spaced 50 cm apart. If the first and last plants in a row are 25 cm from the ends of the row, what is the total number of plants?

answer.worked:
Each row is $1000\text{ cm}$ long.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Distance between first and last plants}&=1000-25-25\\\text{Distance between first and last plants}&=950\text{ cm}\\\text{Number of intervals per row}&=950\div50\\\text{Number of intervals per row}&=19\\\text{Number of plants per row}&=19+1\\\text{Number of plants per row}&=20\\\text{Total number of plants}&=12\times20\\\text{Total number of plants}&=240\end{align*}$$

There is one more plant than the number of intervals between plants.

classification.difficultyReason: Count leap days across nineteen years and interpret the remainder after division by seven.

content.prompt: If 14 January 2006 was a Saturday, what day of the week will 14 January 2025 be?

answer.short:
Tuesday.

The elapsed days leave a remainder of 3 when divided by 7, so advance three weekdays from Saturday.
answer.worked:
The interval contains 19 years. The leap days occur in 2008, 2012, 2016, 2020 and 2024, giving 5 extra days.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Elapsed days}&=19\times365+5\\\text{Elapsed days}&=6940\\6940&=7\times991+3\end{align*}$$

The interval is 991 whole weeks and 3 days. Three days after Saturday is Tuesday.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine unequal journey times over equal distances to calculate the average speed of the whole trip.

content.prompt: My average walking speed up a mountain was 3 km/h. I then ran down the same mountain at a speed of 12 km/h. What was my average speed for the entire trip up and down the mountain?

answer.short:
$4.8\text{ km/h}$

Divide the total distance by the total time for both legs.
answer.worked:
Take the one-way distance as $12\text{ km}$; any equal distance for both legs gives the same average speed.

$$\begin{align*}\text{Time uphill}&=12\div3=4\text{ h}\\\text{Time downhill}&=12\div12=1\text{ h}\\\text{Total distance}&=12+12=24\text{ km}\\\text{Total time}&=4+1=5\text{ h}\\\text{Average speed}&=\frac{24}{5}\text{ km/h}\\\text{Average speed}&=4.8\text{ km/h}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Unshaded hexagon consisting of lower-left and upper-right square regions and two intervening right triangles. Retains both red dashed construction segments, all four 4 cm labels and all three right-angle marks. Decorative blue boundary ink is replaced with house black.
spec.mathematics: Boundary vertices in a centimetre coordinate model are (0,0), (4,0), (8,4), (8,8), (4,8), (0,4). Construction segments x=4 and y=4 meet perpendicularly. The two square regions have side 4 cm and both triangular regions have perpendicular legs 4 cm.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens and supplied construction lines are visible; no calculated areas or extra dimensions appear.

answer.short:
$48\text{ cm}^2$.

Add two squares and two right triangles, or subtract two right triangles from an enclosing square.
answer.worked:
Method 1: add the areas. The dashed lines divide the figure into two squares of side $4$ cm and two right triangles, each with base and perpendicular height $4$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=2(4\times4)+2\left(\frac12\times4\times4\right)\\\text{Area}&=32+16\\\text{Area}&=48\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$
Method 2: subtract the areas. Complete an enclosing square of side $4+4=8$ cm. The two missing corner triangles each have base and perpendicular height $4$ cm.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Area}&=8\times8-2\left(\frac12\times4\times4\right)\\\text{Area}&=64-16\\\text{Area}&=48\text{ cm}^2\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Imagine you have 16 tiles, each 1 cm square. Draw on grid paper some different rectangles that use all 16 tiles. You know that the area of each rectangle you have drawn is $16\text{ cm}^2$. What is the perimeter of each rectangle, in centimetres?

answer.short:
$1\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$: $34\text{ cm}$; $2\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$: $20\text{ cm}$; $4\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$: $16\text{ cm}$.

Arrange the tiles in rectangular rows, then add the four side lengths.
answer.worked:
The different rectangular arrangements have 1 row of 16 tiles, 2 rows of 8 tiles, or 4 rows of 4 tiles. Turning a rectangle does not give a different arrangement.

For the $1\text{ cm}\times16\text{ cm}$ rectangle:
$$\begin{align*}P&=1+16+1+16\\P&=34\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
For the $2\text{ cm}\times8\text{ cm}$ rectangle:
$$\begin{align*}P&=2+8+2+8\\P&=20\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$
For the $4\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ square:
$$\begin{align*}P&=4+4+4+4\\P&=16\text{ cm}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Imagine that you have a piece of string exactly 24 cm long. On grid paper, draw some different rectangular shapes that can be made using the entire 24 cm piece of string. You know that each of these rectangles has a perimeter of 24 cm. What is the area of each, in square centimetres? How small can you make the area of a rectangle with whole number side lengths? How large?

spec.description: Authored blank grid supplies the grid-paper drawing space requested by the question; the source supplies no printed grid.
spec.mathematics: Students draw rectangles with perimeter 24 cm, choosing and stating a suitable scale.
spec.answerVisibility: No rectangles, dimensions or answers are supplied.

answer.short:
Whole-number dimensions and areas: $1\times11$: $11\text{ cm}^2$; $2\times10$: $20\text{ cm}^2$; $3\times9$: $27\text{ cm}^2$; $4\times8$: $32\text{ cm}^2$; $5\times7$: $35\text{ cm}^2$; $6\times6$: $36\text{ cm}^2$.

Smallest: $11\text{ cm}^2$. Largest: $36\text{ cm}^2$, a square. Adjacent side lengths add to $12$ cm.
answer.worked:
Opposite sides are equal, so half the perimeter is the sum of two adjacent sides:
$$\begin{align*}L+W&=24\div2\\L+W&=12\text{ cm}.\end{align*}$$
Draw rectangles with dimensions $1\times11$, $2\times10$, $3\times9$, $4\times8$, $5\times7$ and $6\times6$ cm. Rotating a rectangle gives the same dimensions and area.

Using $A=L\times W$:
$$\begin{align*}A_{1\times11}&=1\times11=11\text{ cm}^2\\A_{2\times10}&=2\times10=20\text{ cm}^2\\A_{3\times9}&=3\times9=27\text{ cm}^2\\A_{4\times8}&=4\times8=32\text{ cm}^2\\A_{5\times7}&=5\times7=35\text{ cm}^2\\A_{6\times6}&=6\times6=36\text{ cm}^2.\end{align*}$$
These are all positive whole-number side pairs adding to $12$. The smallest area is $11\text{ cm}^2$ for $1$ cm by $11$ cm. The largest area is $36\text{ cm}^2$ for the $6$ cm square.

content.prompt: Investigate the possible perimeters for a rectangle of area $64\text{ m}^2$. Which of the alternatives has the smallest perimeter?

answer.short:
An $8\text{ m}\times8\text{ m}$ square has the smallest perimeter, $32\text{ m}$.

Compare rectangles whose length multiplied by width is $64$.
answer.worked:
Choose dimensions whose product is $64$. Some possibilities are:
$$\begin{align*}
P_{1\times64}&=2(1+64)=130\text{ m}\\
P_{2\times32}&=2(2+32)=68\text{ m}\\
P_{4\times16}&=2(4+16)=40\text{ m}\\
P_{6.4\times10}&=2(6.4+10)=32.8\text{ m}\\
P_{8\times8}&=2(8+8)=32\text{ m}
\end{align*}$$
There are infinitely many possibilities because the side lengths need not be whole numbers. For a fixed area, the smallest perimeter occurs when the length and width are equal. Here, $8\times8=64$, so the square has the smallest perimeter, $32\text{ m}$.

content.prompt: Chase and Lana have 108 m of fencing with which to enclose an area of the schoolyard for a rectangular garden. Explore the possible areas of their garden, and state which alternative has the largest area.

answer.short:
The largest area is $729\text{ m}^2$, for a square measuring $27\text{ m}\times27\text{ m}$.

With a fixed perimeter, the area increases as the adjacent side lengths become closer to equal.
answer.worked:
The two lengths and two widths total $108$ m, so one length and one width total $108\div2=54$ m. Some possible dimensions and areas are:
$$\begin{align*}A_{1\text{ m}\times53\text{ m}}&=1\times53=53\text{ m}^2\\A_{10\text{ m}\times44\text{ m}}&=10\times44=440\text{ m}^2\\A_{20\text{ m}\times34\text{ m}}&=20\times34=680\text{ m}^2\\A_{25\text{ m}\times29\text{ m}}&=25\times29=725\text{ m}^2\\A_{26\text{ m}\times28\text{ m}}&=26\times28=728\text{ m}^2\\A_{26.5\text{ m}\times27.5\text{ m}}&=26.5\times27.5=728.75\text{ m}^2\\A_{27\text{ m}\times27\text{ m}}&=27\times27=729\text{ m}^2\end{align*}$$
For a fixed sum of adjacent side lengths, bringing the lengths closer together increases their product. This also applies to fractional side lengths. The largest area therefore occurs when the lengths are equal: a $27$ m by $27$ m square, with area $729\text{ m}^2$.

CHAPTER 9
Measurement and Geometry
Measurement
entries.exclusionReason: Chapter cover and topic identification; no practice question.

entries.description: When we are building a table, hanging a picture on the wall, taking some cough mixture, timing a race and so on, we need to be able to make measurements. Measuring allows us to determine how big, how long, how deep or how heavy things are. Sometimes all we need is a rough idea of a measurement. For example, we might walk along the edge of a garden to measure its length in paces or use a handspan to decide if a table will fit in a certain place in our home. Usually, though, we need a more accurate idea of a measurement. We need to be able to select the right tool and the correct unit to make a measurement, read the scale accurately, and make calculations involving measurements.

entries.description: In order to make a meaningful measurement of some quantity, we need an appropriate unit of measurement. For example, when measuring a person’s mass, we normally use the kilogram as the unit. On the other hand, if we needed to weigh a mosquito, we would generally use a smaller unit, such as the gram or milligram.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation of suitable measurement units; retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: In Australia, we use the metric system of measurement. In this system, the basic units of length, mass and time are the metre (m), the kilogram (kg) and the second (s), respectively.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation of metric units; retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: Apart from some aspects of time measurement, the metric system is a decimal system. (We will discuss time measurement in Section 9I.) Other metric units of length and mass are derived from the basic ones by multiplying or dividing by powers of 10. We indicate the particular power of 10 that we are using by putting a prefix in front of the basic unit. The prefixes most commonly used are: kilo-, denoting 1000; centi-, denoting 1/100; and milli-, denoting 1/1000. So, for example, as well as measuring lengths in metres, we also commonly use kilometres, centimetres and millimetres.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation of metric prefixes; retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: When making a measurement, it is important to choose a suitable unit so that we can clearly picture what we are measuring. For example, it is not very helpful to be told that a person weighs 0.076 tonnes, but we can easily picture what is meant when we are told that he or she weighs 76 kg.

entries.description:
If 5 apples cost $2.50, how much do 3 apples cost?
The easiest way to solve this is to work out the cost of 1 apple and multiply by 3.
5 apples cost $2.50
1 apple costs $0.50   ÷ 5
3 apples cost $1.50   × 3
This method of solving problems is known as the unitary method, because we work out the cost of one item (or unit) first.

entries.exclusionReason: Main topic heading for standalone teaching; no practice questions appear on this page.

entries.description: The area of a rectangle is the size of the region inside it. We measure the area of a rectangle by counting the number of unit squares inside it.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone definition retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: An unshaded rectangle divided into 4 columns and 3 rows of unit squares. The left side is labelled 3 m and the bottom side 4 m. Outer boundary is blue; internal grid lines are black and dashed.
entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram belonging to excluded standalone teaching.

entries.description:
The area of the above rectangle is 12 square metres, which we write as 12 m². We can also find the area of this rectangle by multiplying the lengths of the sides.
Area = 3 × 4
     = 12 m²
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation and supplied calculation retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: We calculate the area of a rectangle by taking the product of the lengths of two adjacent sides. These two sides are called the length and width of the rectangle. It does not really matter which is which, because if we turn the rectangle through 90° and so interchange the length and width, we still have the same area.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: An unshaded landscape rectangle with a blue boundary, labelled Width beside the left side and Length beneath the bottom side.
entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram belonging to excluded standalone teaching.

entries.description:
If we use the letter L to represent the length, and W to represent the width, then we write the area as:
Area = L × W
     = LW
This is called the formula for the area of a rectangle because it applies to all rectangles.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone formula and explanation retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description: When using this formula to calculate the area of a rectangle, we have to make sure that we use the same units for length and width. For example, if we measure the length and width of a rectangle in centimetres (cm), the unit of area is the square centimetre, which is written as cm² because we are multiplying cm by cm.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation of consistent length units and square area units retained as teaching evidence.

entries.description:
Note that we can use the formula for the area of a rectangle to calculate the area of a square, because a square is just a rectangle with equal side lengths.

The length of this square is 3 cm and its width is 3 cm. The area of the square is given by the formula as:
Area = L × W

entries.description:
Commonly used units of area are:
• the square centimetre (cm²), which is the area of a 1 cm by 1 cm square
• the square millimetre (mm²), which is the area of a 1 mm by 1 mm square
• the square metre (m²), which is the area of a 1 m by 1 m square
• the square kilometre (km²), which is the area of a 1 km by 1 km square, and
• the hectare (ha), which is the area of a 100 metre by 100 metre square. This is equivalent to 10 000 m². There are 100 ha in a square kilometre.

entries.description:
The diagram on the right shows a right rectangular prism. Note that:
• the base is a rectangle
• if we slice it through any horizontal plane, the cross-section is a rectangle exactly the same as the base
• there are three right angles at each corner.
(The word ‘right’ is used here as a compact and convenient way of saying ‘the walls are vertical’.)
An example of such a solid is a shoe box.
If the faces are all exactly the same, we call the solid a cube.

The volume of a rectangular prism is a measure of the space inside the prism.

entries.description:
We can cut the prism up into cubes, each of side length 1, as shown. We say that the volume of each of these cubes is 1, which we read as ‘one cubic unit’.

entries.description:
Slices and area
We can see that the rectangular prism is made up of five copies of the 4 × 3 × 1 slice shown. The base area of the slice is 4 × 3 = 12 and the height is 1. There are 5 such slices in the original prism, so we obtain:
Volume = 12 × 5
= 60, as before.
Thus:
Volume = Ah,
where A is the area of the base.
The base can be any one of the six different faces of the prism.
Note: The formulas above are still valid even when the dimensions of the prism are not whole numbers.

entries.description: If the speed of an object does not change, we say that the object is moving with constant speed. entries.description: Kaelah travelled at an (average) speed of 50 km/h for 3 hours. How far did she travel?
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone worked example; retain as taught-method evidence only.

entries.description:
An average speed of 50 km/h means that in 1 hour Kaelah travelled 50 km.
Hence, in 3 hours she travelled 3 × 50 = 150 km.
entries.exclusionReason: Supplied worked-example solution; reference evidence only.

entries.description: The speed of light is approximately 300 000 000 metres per second. How far, in kilometres, would a light ray travel in one minute?
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone worked example; retain as taught-method evidence only.

entries.description:
In one second, light travels 300 000 000 metres.
Hence, in 60 seconds light travels
300 000 000 × 60 metres = 18 000 000 000 metres
= 18 000 000 kilometres

entries.description: Calculate the perimeter and area of figure b.
